input.question: Does eating dirt as a child have any proven benefits for your immune system?
input.ground_truth: Not so much a boosted immune system, but polio affected the upper and middle class far worse than the lower class because kids were exposed to the virus early on in low income areas. As a consequence they became immune to it, while the upper class kids were exposed later in life when it had a far more deleterious effect. [source](_URL_0_)

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Does eating dirt as a child have any proven benefits for your immune system?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you’re asking about eating dirt like some kids want to do when they’re playing outside.

Here’s how I’d explain it to a 5-year-old:

“Sometimes, you might want to eat a little bit of dirt when you’re playing, but grown-ups say it’s not safe. Eating dirt can have tiny things in it that can make you sick, like germs or bugs you can’t see. 

Now, some people think that eating a little bit of dirt might help your body get stronger against sickness, kind of like how eating some germs can help your body learn and fight them better. But scientists have not found a special way that eating dirt helps your body. Actually, it’s safer to let your body learn from clean things, like washing your hands and playing outside, but not eating the dirt.

So, it’s better not to eat dirt, because it can make you sick instead of helping you.”
